calc(1.625em * 1);"><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">Emerging Metrics</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">Given the productivity paradox, metrics to measure productivity and transformation, must be resilient to the paradox:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">AI-First MAU:</span></strong><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);"> 75% or more of code AI-generated. Agent-assisted diffs: aim for at least 55% to see meaningful productivity gains. L4-plus AI tool adoption: 80% or more weekly active usage across engineering functions.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">For business impact, tie AI usage and productivity gains directly to revenue.</span></strong><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);"> Track feature velocity, where the 2 to 10x improvements in prototype-to-production timelines show up. And measure developer experience (satisfaction, flow state, collaboration effectiveness) right alongside the output metrics.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">Quality has to be a core metric, not just a guardrail.</span></strong><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);"> Watch for “AI slop,” the gradual degradation of a codebase as AI-generated code piles up without adequate review. This is the “nobody’s problem” phenomenon, and it can quietly undermine an entire codebase.</span></p></li></ul><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">Transformation Anti-Patterns</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">Eight patterns that consistently derail transformation need special attention from every AI-native leader:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">Tool bolt-on:</span></strong><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);"> AI tools bolted on without redesigning the workflow, producing minimal impact. This is the most common failure mode.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">Review bottleneck:</span></strong><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);"> Traditional review steps become the throughput limit once AI accelerates generation.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">Prompt cargo culting:</span></strong><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);"> Teams copy external prompts without context and get poor agent performance. The bottleneck is context engineering skill, not the model.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">Metrics gaming:</span></strong><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);"> Teams optimize for agent-generated code percentage or adoption stats instead of outcomes.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">Security shortcuts:</span></strong><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);"> Privileged agents deployed without proper audit controls. Some of the resulting production incidents are real and expensive.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">Knowledge debt:</span></strong><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);"> Verification and specification fall behind agent-generated work, creating maintainability risk that compounds over time.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">Junior pipeline hollowing:</span></strong><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);"> Early-career developer experience degrades when human validation gets outsourced to agents. The “missing rung” talent pipeline problem turns into a long-term sustainability risk.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">Meeting creep:</span></strong><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);"> AI acceleration paradoxically makes room for more frequent syncs with no clear impact. The coordination overhead swallows the time that the faster generation saves.</span></p></li></ul><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px months)</span></h2><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">Leadership credibility:</span></strong><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);"> Use AI personally every day with measurable goals. Target 50% or more of your daily tasks within 30 days, then push higher. Get hands-on mastery of the tools so your understanding is authentic. Share both successes and failures in public to model the learning mindset.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">Agent Champion designation:</span></strong><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);"> Identify high-agency technical leaders who can dedicate 50 to 100% of their time. Pull leaders and individual contributors closer together for faster decisions. Set up cross-functional coordination so the whole end-to-end workflow gets transformed.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">Pilot pod formation:</span></strong><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);"> Start with a codebase AI readiness assessment. Form 3 to 5-person cross-functional teams with autonomous operation charters. Aim them at real problems, not toy exercises, so the momentum is genuine.</span></p></li></ul><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">Phase 2: Systematic Redesign (the next couple of months)</span></h2><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">Workflow transformation: </span></strong><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">Audit the high-friction manual workflows that are good candidates for AI. Move from human-in-the-loop to human-on-the-loop. Build AI-readable documentation and specification systems that turn tribal knowledge into shared knowledge.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">Cultural transformation: </span></strong><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">Establish psychological safety: MIT research found 83% of leaders believe psychological safety measurably improves AI initiative success. Formalize “AI failure story” sessions. Shift measurement from output to outcome.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">Technical foundation: </span></strong><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">Clear out dead code, technical debt, and documentation debt to improve AI readiness. Implement sandboxing controls, audit mechanisms, and automated security checks. Build the verification layers that autonomous AI operation depends on.</span></p></li></ul><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">Phase 3: Structural Evolution (everything after)</span></h2><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">Flatten hierarchies:</span></strong><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);"> Remove the coordination layers that slow AI-accelerated work. AI-native builders and AI-native leaders are what you need (consider the STO model).</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">Impact-based progression:</span></strong><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);"> Reward leverage and outcomes over team size. Define the success metrics that genuinely matter for your organization, and make AI tools and agents your highest-leverage assets.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">Cross-functional fluency:</span></strong><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);"> Let roles flex as AI removes traditional skill barriers. Break down the walls between product management, design, engineering, data science, and field support, so AI-native builders can move fluidly and accelerate their builds.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">Throughout the process, track the compounding gains that show up beyond the initial productivity bump. Connect AI adoption to strategic business metrics. And hold quality standards rigorously, because velocity without quality is a negative value.</span></p><h1 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(2em * 1);"><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">Leadership Assessment: Five Questions That Reveal Your Readiness</span></h1><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">Impact scaling:</span></strong><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);"> If you shipped 10x faster, would users be 10x happier? If not, you may be optimizing the wrong thing.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">Empathy depth:</span></strong><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);"> Do you understand your users well enough to delete half the interface? Without empathy, more AI-generated features will not fix products that make users feel incompetent.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">Learning velocity:</span></strong><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);"> Are you processing real user behavioral data every week? If not, your bottleneck is cycle time to insight, not cycle time to code.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">Ownership clarity</span></strong><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">: Does every major initiative have a single owner? Ownership problems wearing a process-problem costume only get worse under AI acceleration.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">Hypothesis discipline:</span></strong><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);"> Are you testing theses or building products? If you cannot name the signal that would kill your project, you are committed to something with no user validation behind it.</span></p></li></ol><h1 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(2em * 1);"><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">AI-Native Process Optimization: The Final Leadership Imperative</span></h1><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">Here is the counterintuitive truth: AI does not reduce the need for process, it changes what the process is for.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">Pre-AI processes coordinated execution among humans. AI compresses execution while raising the cost of deciding what is worth executing. The world now runs on simultaneous builds, parallel experiments, and stacks of prototype iterations. The leadership decisions about what matters, what to cut, and what to double down on become the binding constraint.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">Process optimization comes down to three questions:</span></p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><em><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">What are we learning this week? </span></em><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">Reward faster, deeper learning across teams.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><em><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">What are we killing this week?</span></em><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);"> Actively retire the products and agents that lack genuine value.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><em><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">Who owns each bet, and what signal would change their mind? </span></em><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">STOs steer on objective signals, not intuition and not AI-generated content.</span></p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">Everything else is overhead.</span></p><h1 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(2em * 1);"><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">How Do You Want to Lead in the AI-Native Era?</span></h1><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">The window for this transformation is narrowing. Organizations that pull it off within the next year will open a 5 to 10x productivity gap over the ones that delay, and that gap will be brutally hard to close as AI-native practices compound.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">The organizations that succeed show real advantages in product development velocity, technical innovation capacity, and their ability to attract top talent. The early-mover results (2.4x velocity improvements, 60%-plus AI-generated code, features built in hours instead of days) point to a fundamental capability shift rather than an incremental one. A few closing thoughts.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">The scarce resource has shifted.</span></strong><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);"> It went from generation and production to orchestration and judgment. When AI generates at near-zero marginal cost, the ability to evaluate quality, set direction, and make the hard calls becomes the bottleneck. Leaders who invest in building AI-native team capability will significantly outperform those who just deploy more agents.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">Structural change is mandatory.</span></strong><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);"> The productivity paradox is real. Individual gains do not become organizational gains without redesigning the workflows, the measurement systems, and the cultural norms. Remember the famous line, “culture eats strategy for breakfast,” only shines brighter under the AI light. No amount of transformation will save you if the foundations and the structure are not redesigned for the AI-native era.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">Risk mitigation is continuous, not a one-time fix.</span></strong><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);"> Monitor AI-generated code quality and maintainability so technical debt does not accumulate. Address the security risks (prompt injection, memory corruption, access control, audit compliance) through embedded CI/CD checks. Prevent the “missing rung” talent pipeline problem by developing AI-native engineers at every level. And hold on to human values while you embrace AI acceleration, because human capital keeps paying dividends in the AI-native era when it is applied well.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-bottom: 0;"><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">AI changes the tools. It does not change the core reality. The hard part stays </span><strong><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">insanely human</span></strong><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">.</span></p></div></div><div class="postscript-placeholder" style="margin: 32px 0 0;width: 100%;box-sizing: border-box;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"></div><table class="email-ufi-2-bottom" item.description: AI-Native Leaders: The Organizational Playbook for Engineering Transformation at Scale

item.title: Banned book library
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Banned book library

Rick Osgood

34 minutes by Rick Osgood A hacked WiFi smart light bulb can secretly host banned books as a public digital library. The bulb creates an open WiFi access point, and anyone nearby can connect and browse the books through a web browser. The project uses a cheap ESP32 based smart bulb flashed with custom firmware, with storage expanded by repartitioning the 4MB chip. The 4MB limit means only a few books fit, but that turns each bulb into a personal statement about what its creator finds worth preserving. AURI catches the security issues your AI coding agent introduces
item.description: Banned book library

item.title: Six SQL patterns I use to catch transaction fraud
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Six SQL patterns I use to catch transaction fraud

Fixel Smith

10 minutes by Fixel Smith Fraud detection usually comes down to SQL, not fancy machine learning. Fixel shares six core query patterns which cover most cases: transaction velocity, impossible geographic travel, suspicious amounts, compromised merchants, off-hours activity, and window functions that combine the others. No single pattern is enough on its own, but transactions that fail three or four checks are almost always fraud. Start with velocity, then build from there.
item.description: Six SQL patterns I use to catch transaction fraud

item.title: Stop using Conventional Commits
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Stop using Conventional Commits

Sumner Evans

9 minutes by Sumner Evans Conventional Commits puts commit type like "fix" or "feat" before scope, but scope is what developers actually need when reading logs. Type is usually obvious from the description anyway. The promised benefits like auto-generated changelogs and version bumping fail in practice because changelogs and commit logs serve different audiences with different needs. Projects like Linux and Git use simple scope-first commit messages and work far better.
item.description: Stop using Conventional Commits

item.title: How 2004 RuneScape fit a multiplayer RPG into 56k dial-up
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
How 2004 RuneScape fit a multiplayer RPG into 56k dial-up

James Monger

26 minutes by James Monger James explains how RuneScape supported thousands of players on slow 56k dial-up connections. Using examples from a decompiled game client, he shows how Jagex minimized network traffic through bit-packing, relative coordinates, compact updates, and shared client-server logic. James also highlights how careful protocol design reduced data transfer while maintaining a large multiplayer world, offering lessons that remain relevant for modern networked systems.
item.description: How 2004 RuneScape fit a multiplayer RPG into 56k dial-up

item.title: Stop using JWTs
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Stop using JWTs

Luminessa Starlight

3 minutes by Luminessa Starlight Luminessa argues that JWTs are unsuitable for user authentication sessions because they are designed for short-lived tokens and introduce security and management challenges. She recommends traditional cookie-based sessions as a safer, more efficient solution. For short-lived signed tokens, she suggests using PASETO instead of JWTs. item.title: publishing
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
publishing

Hamed Salameh

Saving data and publishing a message are two separate operations, so a crash between them can silently lose events. The Outbox Pattern fixes this by writing messages to a database table in the same transaction as your business data, then using a background dispatcher to publish them to the broker. This gives you at-least-once delivery without any distributed coordination. Hamed walks through a full .NET 10 implementation using EF Core, PostgreSQL, RabbitMQ, and MassTransit. See one of the few solutions purpose-built for generating real
item.description: publishing

item.title: vulnerability reports
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
vulnerability reports

Nikolche Kolev

.NET 10 now removes platform-provided packages from dependency graphs by default. Many libraries pull in packages like System.Text.Json as dependencies even when the .NET runtime already includes a newer version, causing false vulnerability warnings. Package pruning strips these redundant entries at restore time, cutting false-positive vulnerability reports by 70% and reducing restore times by up to 50%.
item.description: vulnerability reports

item.title: EF Core in clean architecture the pragmatic way
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
EF Core in clean architecture the pragmatic way

Anton Martyniuk

Wrapping EF Core in a repository layer adds unnecessary complexity since DbContext already implements those patterns. Using DbContext directly in application use cases keeps code simpler, easier to read, and faster to change. Tests improve too, as running against a real database with tools like Testcontainers catches bugs that mocked repositories miss. Custom repositories still make sense for complex shared queries, multiple data sources, or strict team conventions.
item.description: EF Core in clean architecture the pragmatic way

item.title: New lines are more than \r and \n
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
New lines are more than \r and \n

Gérald Barré

Most developers only think of \r\n and \n as line breaks, but Unicode defines several more, including \u0085, \u2028, and \u2029. Ignoring these can cause parsing bugs when handling text from office tools, legacy systems, or cross-platform sources. In .NET, you can handle all cases using a regex pattern, string.ReplaceLineEndings, or the SplitLines helper from Meziantou.Framework. item.description: New lines are more than \r and \n

item.title: rows without the wait
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
rows without the wait

Chris Woodruff

Inserting large volumes of data with a simple foreach loop works fine locally but falls apart in production due to slow change tracking, too many database round trips, and high memory use. EF Core 10's native AddRange with a single SaveChangesAsync call solves most of this through batching and fixes the change tracker overhead. For higher volumes or complex parent-child data, Entity Framework Extensions adds bulk insert methods that match raw SQL speed while keeping EF Core model integration. Here's how SLMs and LLMs differ across the dimensions that matter in production: </span></p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span data-color="rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.9)" style="color: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.9);">Architecture: SLMs are usually under 10B parameters and run on a laptop or phone. LLMs handle difficult math, multi-step code, and long-horizon planning. </span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span data-color="rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.9)" style="color: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.9);">Long Context Recall: SLMs lose the thread across long documents or extended conversations. LLMs reliably track and connect information across large inputs.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span data-color="rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.9)" style="color: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.9);">Latency and Cost: SLMs run on consumer hardware with low response times and significantly lower inference costs. LLMs require GPU and carry higher costs per request.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span data-color="rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.9)" style="color: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.9);">Deployment and Privacy: SLMs run on-device or on-premise. LLMs are typically cloud-hosted, which adds data governance complexity.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span data-color="rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.9)" style="color: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.9);"><span>Where each fits:</span><br><span>SLMs: on-device assistants, real-time classification, or privacy-sensitive applications</span><br><span>LLMs: complex reasoning, agent workflows, or broad knowledge tasks.</span></span></p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span data-color="rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.9)" style="color: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.9);"><span>Are you using SLMs, LLMs, or a hybrid setup in production?</span><br></span></p><div style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><hr style="margin: 32px 0;padding: 0;height: 1px;background: rgb(0,0,0,.1);border: none;"></div><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span data-color="rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.9)" style="color: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.9);">Single Agent vs. Multi-Agent Architecture</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span data-color="rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.9)" style="color: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.9);">Some tasks need a single agent. Use a single agent when:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span data-color="rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.9)" style="color: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.9);">the task is a clear, linear sequence</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span data-color="rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.9)" style="color: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.9);">one agent can hold the whole problem in its head</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span data-color="rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.9)" style="color: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.9);">you want something simple to build and easy to debug</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span data-color="rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.9)" style="color: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.9);">Multi-agent system: An orchestrator that splits a task into subtasks and routes each one to a specialized agent. Use multi-agent when:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span data-color="rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.9)" style="color: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.9);">subtasks can run in parallel</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span data-color="rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.9)" style="color: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.9);">one agent writes and another independently verifies the work</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span data-color="rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.9)" style="color: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.9);">the problem is too big for one agent to coordinate alone</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span data-color="rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.9)" style="color: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.9);">Single agents are cheaper and easier to build, but they hit a ceiling on complex work.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span data-color="rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.9)" style="color: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.9);">Multi-agent systems are more capable and more reliable, but they add coordination cost.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span data-color="rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.9)" style="color: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.9);">Start with a single agent. Move to multi-agent only when context or reliability become the bottleneck. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span data-color="rgba(0, item.title: Revised Rules Of Engineering Leadership
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Revised Rules Of Engineering Leadership

Will Larson

“This post documents the new rules I’ve revised my approach to engineering leadership around, and then talks through the specific projects I’ve worked on over the past year that caused me to believe in these rules.”

#Leadership Management
item.description: Revised Rules Of Engineering Leadership

item.title: Don't Stack Weaknesses
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Don't Stack Weaknesses

Yue Zhao

“The real damage happens when you stack weaknesses - when a leader is weak at something and their direct reports are weak at the same thing. This is a disaster, and it happens far more often than you’d think. Part of the reason for this is that leaders tend to hire people with the same skills they have. They’ll dress it up as hiring for “values” instead of “skills” so it doesn’t look like they’re cloning themselves - but people ultimately search for and evaluate the things they’re good at.”

#Management Hiring
item.description: Don't Stack Weaknesses

item.title: Why Spreading Yourself Thin Feels Like Winning
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Why Spreading Yourself Thin Feels Like Winning

Steve Huynh

“Every “yes” is a check written against the future that has to be cleared. And clearing checks written by “powerful Us” is especially tough. Why? Because, by definition, we are only average most of the time. This article provides a guide to recognizing overextension in ourselves, so that, before we commit to things, we can be sure that we are only taking on what we can hold.”

#CareerGrowth DecisionMaking Wellbeing
item.description: Why Spreading Yourself Thin Feels Like Winning

item.title: The Worst Take In Tech: New Grad Hiring
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
The Worst Take In Tech: New Grad Hiring

Scott Kennedy

“In this generation we call them “AI Natives”. The advantage is that there are no old habits to break or reframe. Many experienced folks are open minded and can do it, but many resist. New grads don’t know the difference, their learning came in parallel to having these tools. We see it in interviews regularly, new grads can use AI coding tools incredibly well.”

#IndustryTrends AI Hiring
item.description: The Worst Take In Tech: New Grad Hiring

item.title: Why Is Meta Destroying Its Engineering Organization?
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Why Is Meta Destroying Its Engineering Organization?

Gergely Orosz

“In this article, we walk through what’s happened, and ask what’s going through the minds of leadership who are reducing software engineering there from the profit center that it was between 2004 until very recently, to the disdained cost center that it has become in just a few weeks.”

#IndustryTrends Leadership
item.description: Why Is Meta Destroying Its Engineering Organization?

item.title: SQLite Improving Performance With Pre-Sort
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
SQLite Improving Performance With Pre-Sort

Anders Murphy

“The defining characteristic of a B+ Tree is that it is ordered. Sequential writes are fast. Random data works against this thrashing pages, causing page splits and tree re-balancing. It's not a good time. But, we are batching the data already. So what if we sort it before we insert?”

#Database DeepDive Performance
item.description: SQLite Improving Performance With Pre-Sort

item.title: Agentic Code Review
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Agentic Code Review

Addy Osmani

“Stop reviewing everything to the same depth. Spend scarce human attention only where being wrong is costly, and let cheap deterministic gates and AI reviewers handle the rest. The organizing idea is to match review effort to the cost of being wrong, push the cheap deterministic work as early as possible, and reserve human attention for what only humans can do.”

#CodeReview AI Agents
item.description: Agentic Code Review

running service generates events constantly.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">Requests arrive, functions run, errors appear, and each one is a thing that happened at a specific time with a specific context and a specific outcome.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">Logs, metrics, and traces are three ways of looking at this same stream. A log captures one event as a line of text, a metric counts or aggregates many events, and a trace links related events as they move across services. Most of the concepts in observability, including cardinality, sampling, and correlation, are consequences of this structure.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">In this article, we will look at the basics of observability in detail with concepts like logs, Rob and I were also once colleagues on the Skype web team, working on large-scale deployments and release processes.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In this episode of</span><em> The</em><span> </span><em>Pragmatic Engineer</em><span>, I sit down with Rob to discuss how teams deploy software safely and efficiently at scale. We cover Kubernetes, GitOps, platform engineering, progressive delivery, feature flags, cloud development environments, and the growing role of AI in CI/CD workflows. We also get into the tradeoffs in different deployment approaches, why self-hosted software still matters for some organizations, and the recent evolution of software delivery practices.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);">Key observations on deployments and CI/CD from the conversation with Rob</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Here are 10 interesting takeaways from our chat:</p><a class="youtube-wrap" href="https://substack.com/redirect/c9ba451e-654c-49a4-95ed-97b607ff898d?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" target="_blank" data-component-name="Youtube2ToDOMStatic" style="display: block;margin: 32px 0;"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/youtube/w_728,c_limit/l_youtube_play_qyqt8q,w_120/2x0eq5oDOJY" style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;max-width: 100%;height: auto;margin: 0 auto;display: block;width: 100%;"></a><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>1. Roll forward, never backwards. </strong><span>When a system has state – which typically means it uses databases – then doing a rollback can leave the code talking to a schema that’s no longer in sync. Rob’s advice is to not treat a failure in v2 as a trip back to v1, but rather as a push to v3 with the fix in it.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>2. GitOps isn’t actually about Git.</strong><span> None of the four pillars of GitOps – 1) declarative, 2) versioned and immutable, 3) pulled, not pushed, 4) continuously reconciled  – require Git, although Git can work under these constraints. Yet, the term  ‘GitOps’ has made the industry dogmatic about cramming </span><em>everything</em><span> into a repo – even things like secrets that absolutely shouldn’t be there!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>3. Continuous deployment can be overkill; continuous delivery is more practical. </strong><span>Shipping every single change to prod (continuous deployment) is not as necessary as many people think, Rob says, and there’s often more value in continuous delivery, where changes flow through testing and the deployment process itself is validated. With continuous delivery, you can decide whether to push to production automatically, or click a button once a week.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>4. Feature toggles are a better safety net than rollbacks.</strong><span> When something breaks in production, reaching for a toggle to switch a feature off enables you to “stop the bleeding” and then calmly diagnose an issue. Rolling back a feature flag is less nerve-jangling than scrambling to force a redeployment in the middle of the night!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>5. One problem with feature flags is that they’re addictive.</strong><span> On the other hand, the ease with which feature flags are added can create a hygiene crisis if they’re continuously added, but not removed. Treat feature-toggle cleanups like a form of gardening and “weed” rolled-out toggles from the codebase.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>6. A Git repo can be a bottleneck at scale.</strong><span> Rob mentions that some companies run thousands of independent Kubernetes clusters that pull state from a Git repository. But such clusters can get throttled by the repo, forcing them into workarounds. Pull-based GitOps doesn’t scale infinitely for free.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>7. A sizable number of major institutions remain on-prem – and this won’t change. </strong><span>Banks, other financial bodies, and governments, demand full control over their hardware, upgrades, and downtime. That’s why Rob expects this segment won’t move to cloud-based SaaS.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>8. Platform teams work at larger companies. </strong><span>These teams earn their keep in big organizations with multiple teams and projects because they offer ways of bringing sanity and focus.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>9. There’s a trend of ephemeral environments replacing test/staging environments. </strong><span>Companies used to have a few testers fighting over a handful of static test environments, but today, it’s trivial to spin up a full environment, per-feature branch, pre-merge. This is an “ephemeral” environment for evaluating that things work, which is then torn down once something is merged. It helps speed up the feedback process.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>10. AI shifts the CI/CD calculus from speed to risk.</strong><span> Today, shaving ten minutes off the CI build-time matters because a long-running build blocks human devs. But this time saving will be insignificant when an AI agent writes most of the code and “babysits” a slow pipeline without context switching. Then, the new priority will be to reduce the risk of an AI agent shipping a bug to production, so it will make much more sense to run extra, more thorough, tests – and also even slower ones.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;">For two decades, Meta had a unique, high-performance engineering org; right up until around April of this year. For the first 20 years of the company’s existence, it had a “move-fast-and-break-things” culture, and in the early 2020s this shifted to a “move-fast-with-stable-infra” one. Engineers I know at the company were empowered to do good work, focus on impact, and to balance business interests with solid engineering.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But in the past few weeks, all that has changed, as if the leadership has been following detailed blueprints on how to demolish a proven, successful engineering culture in the most ruthlessly efficient way possible.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For the past few weeks, I’ve been </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/9fa16a18-4caf-4672-9054-f597f8294b90?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">sharing</a><span> how bad things are inside the social media company for engineers in one of Silicon Valley’s most prestigious workplaces. In this article, we walk through what’s happened, and ask what’s going through the minds of leadership who are reducing software engineering there from </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/ede80667-8416-4522-9609-fb94e61936bc?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">the profit center</a><span> that it was between 2004 until very recently, to the disdained cost center that it has become in just a few weeks.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">We cover:</p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: Meta’s pre-AI engineering culture</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">I’d split Meta’s engineering culture into two eras: “move fast and break things”, and then “move fast with stable infra.”</p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);">“Move fast and break things”</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">In the 2010s, Facebook’s unconventional engineering culture had grown somewhat legendary in the tech industry, as the company went against conventional best practices and succeeded massively.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">In 2012, when Facebook hit the billion-users landmark, the company produced a small physical book about its culture which was placed on employees’ desks. Presented with retro propaganda design, it was dubbed the “little red book”, co-opting the name of a famous volume of the thoughts of Chairman Mao, (1964).</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">At around 70 pages long, Facebook’s version codified its engineering culture: speed, fearlessness, taking ownership, and thinking outside of the
